messages.author: 6bc71e3ba7ba8dff
messages.subject: power analysis using stan_lmer
parts:
Hi, I am currently using stan_lmer to built my model and need to do a power analysis to estimate my sample size. I would like to simulate the parameter of my model several times with different sample sizes to make predictions of how many more subjects I need to measure.

I already have the data of 31 subjects but the confidence interval for my beta is only about 80% away from 0 (so still slightly overlaps).

Please let me know

M

messages.author: fd4f3538f907404b
messages.subject: Re: power analysis using stan_lmer
parts:
On Friday, February 17, 2017 at 2:17:04 PM UTC-5, sfs.s...@googlemail.com wrote:
Hi, I am currently using stan_lmer to built my model and need to do a power analysis to estimate my sample size. I would like to simulate the parameter of my model several times with different sample sizes to make predictions of how many more subjects I need to measure.

I already have the data of 31 subjects but the confidence interval for my beta is only about 80% away from 0 (so still slightly overlaps).

The lme4 package has a simulate method so that you can say e.g.

   simulate(~x+(1|f),newdata=dd,newparams=list(theta=0.5,beta=c(1,1),sigma=1,family=gaussian)

where

- dd is a data frame with predictor variables matching your experimental design;
- theta is a vector of the random-effects parameters (in this case, it's the standard deviation of the among-group variation scaled by the residual standard deviation)
- beta are fixed-effect parameters
- sigma is the random-effects standard deviation

  By the way, what you're suggesting sounds close to "post hoc power analysis", which can when done simplemindedly be foolish.  You should consider not putting in the *observed* effect sizes from your current set of data, but rather the effect sizes/parameters that you *would initially have guessed* (with the possible exception of theta and sigma).

Please let me know

M

messages.author: fc5d3270037d7478
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: power analysis using stan_lmer
parts:
We're planning to add some tools to make this much easier to do with rstanarm. Hopefully we'll have something soon.

One thing that might be interesting for you to do is to fit a model with argument prior_PD = TRUE and then do posterior_predict. That corresponds to drawing from the prior predictive distribution, and you can pass any data.frame/design you want as the newdata argument to posterior_predict.

Jonah
